articles.title: Week 12 fantasy football WR start-sit: Douglas, Meyers, Mitchell, Waddle
articles.summary: Tennessee and Los Angeles have allowed 11 receiver touchdowns over the last three weeks.
articles.body:
Jakobi Meyers and DeMario Douglas are Week 12 fantasy football WR start 'em picks because the Tennessee Titans and Los Angeles Chargers have allowed more than 40 half-PPR points per game to receivers over the last three weeks.

New York Jets receiver Adonai Mitchell and Denver Broncos wideout Jaylen Waddle are sits. The Miami Dolphins allow 22.0 half-PPR points per game to receivers, fourth-fewest in the NFL, and the Pittsburgh Steelers have given up just five touchdowns to wideouts all season.

My Week 12 rankings have Meyers at WR28 and Douglas at WR34. Mitchell is at WR38 and Waddle at WR39.

The Week 11 calls finished 2-2. Both sits landed and both starts fell short.

Starts : Waddle (WR38 finish) caught three of six targets for 61 yards in Denver's 38-24 win over the Las Vegas Raiders, which works out to 7.6 half-PPR points. Mitchell (WR61 finish) caught two of three targets for 30 yards in the Jets' 27-24 win over the Chargers, good for just 4.0 half-PPR points.

Sits : Tre Tucker (WR48 finish) caught two of 10 targets for 50 yards (6.0 half-PPR points) in the Raiders' loss, so benching him paid off. San Francisco 49ers wideout Keenan Allen (WR55 finish) caught three of four targets for 38 yards (5.3 half-PPR points) in a 35-10 rout of the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City. Mike Evans returned in that game and led the team with 109 yards.

Week 12 WR start 'em: Jakobi Meyers, Jaguars

Week 12: vs. Tennessee, 37.2 FP/G to WRs (32nd)

Week 11: at N.Y. Giants, 4 rec. for 85 yds

Meyers drew 10 targets in the Jacksonville Jaguars' 23-18 loss to the New York Giants, matching his season high. His 85 yards were his most this year. He played 83% of the snaps and trailed only Parker Washington in catches, yards and targets.

His ankle bears watching after he was spotted working off to the side at Wednesday's practice. Still, he played through the same issue last week without an injury designation.

No defense is friendlier to receivers than Tennessee. The Titans allow 37.2 half-PPR points per game to wideouts, most in the league. That number jumps to 49.6 over the last five weeks and 53.9 over the last three.

Meyers didn't cash in when these teams met in Nashville two weeks ago. He caught three of six targets for 34 yards in the 40-23 win. Washington still posted seven catches for 152 yards and a touchdown, and rookie Josh Cameron turned three grabs into 67 yards and a score.

Jaguars analyst Bucky Brooks wrote that the passing game " should flourish " in the rematch. With 22 targets over his last three games, Meyers is a confident WR3 at home against a 1-9 team.

Week 12 WR start 'em: DeMario Douglas, Patriots

Week 12: at L.A. Chargers, 29.8 FP/G to WRs (28th)

The New England Patriots come out of their bye without their starting quarterback or A.J. Brown. Drake Maye is out with a lower-leg injury. Coach Mike Vrabel said he doesn't anticipate Brown playing because of a hamstring injury, and Romeo Doubs (shoulder) is still on injured reserve.

Douglas leads New England's wideouts with 32 catches, 438 yards and four touchdowns. The 5-foot-8 slot man has topped 10 half-PPR points in four of his last six games.

Tommy DeVito struggled after replacing Maye in Munich, but he's now had a full week of first-team reps. "I've waited for this moment ," DeVito said. Backup quarterbacks tend to lean on quick, short throws, so Douglas' slot role should get the first look.

The 1-9 Chargers make the quarterback downgrade easier to live with. Los Angeles allows 29.8 points per game to receivers, fifth-most, and 36.8 over the last five weeks, third-most. Wideouts caught 37 passes for 609 yards and seven touchdowns in the Chargers' last three games. Jets practice squad call-up Sterling Shepard scored twice against them on Sunday. Douglas is a WR3 with touchdown upside in three-receiver leagues.

Week 12 WR sit 'em: Adonai Mitchell, Jets

Week 12: at Miami, 22.0 FP/G to WRs (4th)

Week 11: at L.A. Chargers, 2 rec. for 30 yds

I started Mitchell last week against one of the softest receiver matchups in football, and he drew three targets. Omar Cooper Jr. and Isaiah Williams were inactive, but Mitchell still trailed Garrett Wilson's five targets. The Jets called 37 runs and 22 passes.

Mitchell had seven catches for 142 yards against Las Vegas in Week 8. In three games since, he has five catches on 18 targets. His hands haven't helped either, as he leads the league in drop rate at 20.8%.

Miami is a much tougher draw than Los Angeles. The Dolphins allow 22.0 points per game to receivers, fourth-fewest, and wideouts have caught only 98 passes against them in 10 games. Mitchell already faced this defense in Week 7 and didn't catch any of his three targets.

The 3-8 Jets face a 1-9 Dolphins team. If New York gets ahead, Los Angeles will likely return to its run-heavy plan. Mitchell is a boom-or-bust WR4 who needs a long catch to pay off, and that kind of player belongs on the bench this week.

Week 12 WR sit 'em: Jaylen Waddle, Broncos

Week 12: at Pittsburgh, 24.5 FP/G to WRs (9th)

Week 11: vs. Las Vegas, 3 rec. for 61 yds

Waddle's 61 yards against the Raiders were his most since Week 2, and they still added up to only 7.6 half-PPR points. He's scored 7.6 or fewer in five of his last six games. His only double-digit outing without a touchdown was his eight-catch, 138-yard game against Jacksonville in September.

Sean Payton said in early November, "We're going to need his plays down the stretch ," but the volume hasn't followed. Waddle hasn't drawn more than seven targets in a game since Week 2, and Bo Nix spread 19 completions across seven players last week.

Waddle needs a touchdown to pay off, and Pittsburgh rarely allows them. The Steelers give up 24.5 points per game to receivers, ninth-fewest. Their five touchdowns allowed to wideouts are tied for second-fewest in the league, behind only Kansas City.

Denver also has a short week, going from a Sunday game to a Black Friday trip. Bench Waddle if you have a comparable option.

This column is built for 12-team leagues, where lineup decisions happen on the fringe. Telling you to start a WR10 in a great matchup or bench a WR12 in a tough one doesn't help anyone, because those players are in your lineup every week.

Starts come from roughly WR25 to WR36 in my weekly rankings, and sits come from roughly WR37 to WR45. Within those ranges, I'm looking for the easiest and toughest matchups based on points allowed, yards allowed, recent production and the latest news.

Every league is different, so these calls won't fit every roster. They're meant to settle the closest decisions most managers face each week.

articles.title: 'I want us to go all the way': PV Sindhu eyes historic Uber Cup triumph as India gets 2028 hosting rights
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Two-time Olympic medallist PV Sindhu has set her sights on a maiden Uber Cup title for India after the country was awarded the hosting rights
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Two-time Olympic medallist PV Sindhu has set her sights on a maiden Uber Cup title for India after the country was awarded the hosting rights for the 2028 Thomas and Uber Cup Finals, expressing her desire to go few steps further than the bronze medal she won on home soil in 2014.Sindhu was part of the Indian women's squad that created history by securing the country's first-ever Uber Cup medal, a bronze, when New Delhi hosted the tournament in 2014. With the prestigious team championships returning to India after 14 years, the former world champion hopes the next opportunity will bring an even bigger achievement."I was proud of the bronze we won in Delhi in 2014. If I get another chance to play the Uber Cup at home, I want us to go all the way. I know what it meant to stand on that podium with my teammates. To lift the trophy together in front of an Indian crowd would be one of the proudest moments of my career," Sindhu said in a media release.The Badminton World Federation (BWF) announced on Wednesday that India had secured the hosting rights for the 2028 edition, following the successful staging of the 2025 BWF World Junior Championships in Guwahati and the 2026 BWF World Championships in New Delhi.Sindhu hopes to inspire next generationThe 2028 edition will be particularly significant as it will be the first Thomas and Uber Cup Finals to feature an expanded 24-team format, with each tie decided over three matches instead of the traditional five.Sindhu also reflected on the experience of competing at the World Championships in Delhi earlier this year, saying the atmosphere and support from Indian fans had left a lasting impression on visiting players."At the World Championships in Delhi, players from other countries told me how much they enjoyed walking out to that crowd. I felt proud that my generation got to play a World Championships at home."In 2028, an Olympic year, young shuttlers will get to see Team India take on the world's best. I hope they leave the stands determined to earn their place on that court and play for India one day," she added.India's growing stature in team badmintonIndia will host the Thomas and Uber Cup Finals for the second time, having previously staged the competition at the Siri Fort Sports Complex in New Delhi in 2014. The women's side also won bronze in 2016, while the men's team made history by lifting its maiden Thomas Cup title in 2022. India added another men's team bronze at the 2026 edition in Horsens, Denmark.Badminton Association of India secretary general Sanjay Mishra said the latest hosting rights reflected the BWF's confidence in India's ability to stage major international competitions."Securing three of badminton's biggest international championships for India in three years reflects the confidence the BWF has in our ability to deliver. It is a fitting way to close a year in which Indian shuttlers delivered strong results across formats, including a Thomas Cup bronze."When the Finals return to India after 14 years, our players will have the opportunity to compete for a world team title in front of a home crowd," Mishra said.Indian shuttlers have also enjoyed a productive 2026 season, winning a record nine BWF World Tour titles at the Super 300 level or above outside India. The 2028 championships will provide another opportunity for the country to translate its growing strength into a major team title.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The 10 Most Slept-On Matches in WWE Survivor Series History
articles.summary: WWE's Survivor Series premium live event has featured some of the most significant moments in professional wrestling history, as well as some epic encounters over its nearly four decades.
articles.body:
WWE's Survivor Series premium live event has featured some of the most significant moments in professional wrestling history, as well as some epic encounters over its nearly four decades.

It has also been home to some under-the-radar bangers and hidden gems: matches that have been forgotten over time or overshadowed by bigger, more important bouts and moments from their respective broadcasts.

In preparation for the 2026 edition this Saturday from Daikin Park in Houston, Texas, here are the 10 most slept-on matches in the event's long and illustrious history, ranked according to match quality.

10. Dragon Lee vs. Santos Escobar (2023)

Fresh off a heel turn that saw Santos Escobar betray his Latino World Order teammates, he squared off with Dragon Lee in an undercard bout on the 2023 Survivor Series card.

Not a match that had the audience behind it from the get-go, it earned the crowd's investment, thanks to both men's undeniable ability. They were allowed to showcase that ability without incessant run-ins and overbooking, though this would theoretically have been a place where it would have made sense, only enhancing its quality.

Late in the match, Lee powerbombed the hell out of Escobar but could only net a two-count. Escobar recovered, turned the masked competitor inside out with a destroyer, and finished him off with a Phantom Driver for one of his more impressive televised victories.

Historically speaking, the match has zero relevance, but it was a damn good one on a show that concluded with CM Punk making his return after a decade away and overshadowing everything else on the card.

Go track this one down and give it a watch, if for no other reason than understanding how good Escobar was and how inexplicable his lack of a sustained push ended up being.

9. Cruiserweight Championship Match: Mustafa Ali vs. Buddy Murphy (2018)

The revamped cruiserweight division in the mid-2010s may have been an afterthought to everyone behind the scenes in WWE, but the Superstars competing for 205 Live's top prize often went to the ring with the intention of stealing the show.

Few succeeded more often than Buddy Murphy and Mustafa Ali, which is why it was no surprise when they showed up and showed out at the 2018 Survivor Series.

A fast-paced, high-energy, uber-athletic match the likes of which were not present up and down the rest of the card, saw Murphy and Ali make the most of the 12:25 they were allotted and damn near steal the show.

The crowd was not as into the bout early, thanks to the lack of effort put into the cruiserweight division by the company. Still, the athletes won the fans over, thanks to increased intensity down the stretch, a brutal knee from the champion, and his Murphy's Law finisher for the win.

A great hidden gem from the Survivor Series annals, this is more than worth a look and serves as evidence of how disappointingly the company mishandled both stars.

CM Punk's WWE Championship reign should never have ended at SummerSlam 2011 via a Money in the Bank cash-in from Alberto Del Rio.

It was a bad decision then and, in hindsight, is even worse. It threatened to cool off the industry's most popular star at a time when WWE couldn't afford it, making the creative decision even more curious.

At the 2011 Survivor Series, the ship would be righted when Punk challenged Del Rio for the gold in Madison Square Garden.

A good match between two strong workers, it featured plenty of counters and reversals, with neither man able to put the other away with their signature maneuvers.

Then, Punk caught Del Rio in the Anaconda Vise, forced the tapout and regained the gold that never should have left his waist in the first place.

Making the moment that much more special was the post-match announcement from the legendary Howard Finkel, who declared Punk the new WWE champion. It was one of the last times Finkel got to make his signature "new champion" call before his death in April 2020.

Most Likely WWE Survivor Series Face and Heel Turns

1995 was an abyss of bad booking, worse gimmicks, and a year-long run for Diesel as WWE Champion that did the opposite of set the business on fire.

While the idea of a feud between long-time enhancement talent Barry Horowitz and Bodydonna Skip may not have been the most appealing thing to come out of Vince McMahon's creative meetings, but it did result in a feud-ending, 4-on-4 elimination tag match at the Survivor Series.

Horowitz captained the team also featuring Hakushi, Marty Jannetty, and Bob Holly against Skip and his team of Rad Radford, Dr. Tom Prichard, and the freshly-turned-heel 1-2-3 Kid.

An energetic match featuring eight guys who knew how to work, could deliver if given the opportunity, and were far better between the ropes than a large portion of the Superstars higher than them in the pecking order, set the tone for what would become one of the more underrated Survivor Series shows of the decade.

The Kid earned the victory for his team, pinning Jannetty and building heat at a crucial point for his character. For most everyone else, it would be the last real gasp of a push, though Holly would enjoy several more appearances at the annual November extravaganza.

On a night when Steve Austin took his greatest step yet toward superstardom by way of an instant classic with Bret Hart, and a young Rocky Maivia made his first impression on the WWE Universe, it is easy to see why Shawn Michaels and Sycho Sid's main event was overshadowed.

Still, the match was one of the better main events in the show's history; an indictment of the vanilla babyface Michaels and an embrace of the edgy, unpredictable Sid in what was the first indication that what fans demanded from WWE programming was changing.

Between the ropes, Michaels wrestled Sid's style of match, selling and bumping around for the big man, all while the New Yorkers inside the famed Madison Square Garden cheered for the No. 1 contender.

In the closing moments of the match, the dastardly Sid even struck the legendary Jose Lothario with a camera to the chest, which triggered what appeared to be a cardiac event. Michaels, distracted by the condition of his mentor, took his eye off the ball, allowing Sid to capitalize by driving him to the mat with a powerbomb and secure the win.

A worthwhile watch for the crowd's reaction to the story being told and its rejection of Michaels as champion, despite him working his ass off to deliver a fantastic main event with a guy not known for his in-ring skill set.

Take two talented in-ring competitors, give them 18 minutes to work with no shenanigans, and reap the rewards.

That is exactly what happened at the 2022 show when AJ Styles squared off with The Judgment Day's leader, Finn Balor.

Fellow Bullet Club alums from their days in New Japan Pro-Wrestling, the two had plenty of backstory, but one goal: to prove who was better.

There was some brawling between The Good Brothers and Balor's Judgment Day teammates on the arena floor, but for the most part, this was a match focused on its combatants.

A back-and-forth match featuring plenty of reversals, counters, and near-misses for both men, it concluded with The Phenomenal One catching The Prince with an enzuigiri kick in the corner that set up the Phenomenal Forearm for the win.

Not a match with a ton of bells and whistles, this was an example of what Triple H did so well early on in his creative stint: take two guys with history, put them in the ring, and let them wrestle until there was a winner. It was not overthought, overbooked, or marred by interference to protect one or the other.

4. 10-on-10 Tag Team Elimination Match (1987)

The 1987 debut of the Survivor Series event may have been an excuse to bring Hulk Hogan and Andre the Giant together and continue maximizing the profits from that legendary rivalry, but tucked on the undercard was a showcase of the extraordinary WWE tag team division.

An enormous 10-on-10 Tag Team Elimination Match pitted one team consisting of The British Bulldogs, The Young Stallions, The Killer Bees, Strike Force, and The Fabulous Rougeaus against The Hart Foundation, Demolition, The Dream Team, The Bolsheviks, and The Islanders.

A jam-packed field consisting of Hall of Fame talent and all-time-greats captivated fans for 37 minutes, highlighting the power of tag team wrestling in its golden age.

The Killer Bees and Young Stallions earned the win for the babyfaces, building momentum for each team rather than further emphasizing the more prolific teams in the match.

The company would attempt to replicate the match the following year but too much story weighed down the action and hurt the overall quality.

3. Shawn Michaels vs. Randy Orton (2007)

WWE Champion Randy Orton defended his title against Shawn Michaels at the 2007 event, with two major stipulations at play. If Orton got disqualified, he would lose the title. If Michaels utilized Sweet Chin Music, he would be disqualified and never receive another shot at the gold as long as The Legend Killer was champion.

Unable to uncork Sweet Chin Music, Michaels dug deep into his arsenal, pulling out submission moves popularized by some of his most famous opponents, including Bret Hart's Sharpshooter, Chris Benoit's Crossface, and Kurt Angle's ankle lock.

Watching a guy so synonymous with one move have to reinvent himself on the fly to combat a cold, calculating champion made for a fresh take in a repetitive rivalry and created plenty of drama for fans to invest in along the way.

Late, Michaels set up for Sweet Chin Music but pulled the kick at the last second. That momentary distraction allowed Orton to catch him with the RKO and win the match.

A wholly unique take on a Michaels match from that era, it is one of this writer's favorites and proof of the Heartbreak Kid's excellence.

2. WWE Championship Match: Bret Hart vs. Shawn Michaels (1992)

One mention of "Survivor Series" brings about the images of Bret Hart and Shawn Michaels warring in Montreal, home of the most infamous double-cross in pro wrestling history.

Five years earlier, though, the Hitman and Heartbreak Kid entered unfamiliar territory: headlining a WWE pay-per-view as two of the young stars selected to carry the company in to the next generation.

Hart had recently captured the top prize in the company from Ric Flair while Michaels had bested his opponent's brother-in-law, the British Bulldog, for the Intercontinental Championship.

For 26 minutes, the two celebrated in-ring performers delivered a main event unlike anything fans of the company had seen in years, especially with Hulk Hogan and the Ultimate Warrior on top.

Hart overcame a focused and intent Michaels, trapping him in the Sharpshooter and forcing the submission for the win and successful title defense. Win or lose, it was clear that the third-generation star and his Survivor Series opponent would form the foundation of wrestling's future.

Even if there were a few roadblocks to overcome in the years that followed.

1. Last Man Standing Match: Ric Flair vs. Triple H (2005)

The mid-2000s are not necessarily a hotbed of forgotten matches. Due to the nature of the era, what's great is memorable, and what is not is, well, not. There is a majorly slept-on match from the 2005 Survivor Series, though, that remains one of the event's best of the last quarter-century.

It doesn't get nearly the love that it should, despite featuring two of the biggest and most influential stars of all time: Ric Flair and Triple H. The culminating match of their underrated rivalry, mentor and protege squared off in a Last Man Standing Match.

The former teammates in Evolution beat each other up and down, brutalizing one another in an attempt to keep them down for the referee's count. Late in the match, his body wracked with pain, a defiant and bloodied Flair flipped The Cerebral Assassin the bird, daring him to put him down.

And Triple H did, delivering a sledgehammer shot to the face that earned him the win.

A great example of Flair as the resilient babyface, who absorbed all that he could until he could not anymore, it was a brilliant match that intertwined story in it seamlessly without taking away from the action itself, something today's product could use more of.
